newsitem.title: KENYA: Armed police patrol Nairobi after riots, 133 arrested.
newsitem.headline: Armed police patrol Nairobi after riots, 133 arrested.

text.p: Hundreds of heavily-armed police patrolled a section of Kenya's capital on Monday as the government blamed street hawkers for weekend rioting.
But a leading opposition parliamentarian said authorities provoked the riots by breaking up a peaceful opposition rally on Saturday called to press for constitutional change.

Riot police equipped with long staves, helmets and shields patrolled the run-down lower business district backed by truckloads of police deployed visibly to prevent a third day of rioting and to stop hawkers from displaying their merchandise.
At least 133 people were arrested during weekend rioting and would be charged with "criminal offences", the government said in a statement read on state-run radio and television.
"Hawkers and idlers actively participated in the acts of lawlessness triggered by the illegal meeting organized by the opposition activists," the statement said.
"Hawking in the Nairobi city centre's business district has therefore been banned and hawkers are ordered to evacuate the streets with immediate effect," it said.
A government order last month that street traders relocate to designated areas outside the centre was largely ignored.
A total of 22 policemen and dozens of civilians were injured during the rioting, 61 shops were looted, two cars were burnt and dozens of others stoned, the government said.
One person was stabbed to death on Saturday after security forces broke up a banned rally called by opposition leaders and church groups demanding constitutional reform.
The riot continued on a smaller scale in the run-down outer business district on Sunday.
Monday, a public holiday in Kenya, the capital was calm, but Nairobians anticipated trouble later in the day on account of the police build-up in the city.

"I think that the (government) statement is hogwash... Hawkers have been in town for a long time and there has been no rioting," Raila Odinga, leader of the National Development Party of Kenya told Reuters.
"The people were reacting to extreme provocation by the police and now they want to blame it on opposition supporters."
Odinga said the shadowy "Jeshi la Mzee" (Moi's army) group of youths supposedly recruited by the ruling party to cause trouble was behind much of the looting.
President Daniel arap Moi told a state rally on Sunday there could be no constitutional change before elections later this year, resisting demands by opposition and church leaders.
He also said the Public Order Act, which regulates public meetings but is widely seen as repressive, would be replaced with a new bill but gave no details of how it would differ.

Opposition leaders including Odinga, who were detained in their houses on Sunday to prevent protest during the state rally, rejected Moi's statement and vowed to continue defying the law in support of constitutional change.
The opposition would hold a news conference later on Monday to respond formally to Moi's speech, Odinga said.
A coalition of opposition parties, human rights groups and church leaders under the National Convention Assembly want six pre-independence laws, including the Public Order Act, scrapped.
They also demand greater access to state-run media and an Independent Electoral Commission.

Moi, Kenya's president since 1978, must call elections before the end of the year, pitting his ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party against an opposition fractured by ethnic and personal differences.
